title: Chest tightness and palpitations in an anxious 29-year-old woman
opening_brief:
You are a medical student in the emergency department.

A 29-year-old woman has presented with chest tightness and a racing heart. She tells the triage nurse she has had panic attacks before and thinks this is another one.

Assess her. Be careful: an explanation the patient offers you is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis.

patient.name: Ananya Rao
patient.background: Recently returned from a work trip. Under pressure at work.

persona.speech_style: Fast, slightly breathless, apologetic. Keeps saying she is probably wasting everyone's time.
persona.emotional_state: Anxious and embarrassed. Becomes more forthcoming if the student is reassuring.
knows_not: what a blood clot in the lung feels like
the name of her contraceptive pill brand beyond 'the daily one'
quirks: Volunteers 'I get panic attacks' more than once, because she genuinely believes it.
Mentions the flight only if asked about travel, immobility or the last few weeks.

chief_complaint: chest tightness and a racing heart since yesterday evening

present_illness.onset: Started yesterday evening while sitting at her desk. Nothing in particular set it off.
present_illness.site: Right side of the chest, more towards the side than the middle.
present_illness.character: Tight, and also a catching pain when she breathes in deeply.
present_illness.duration: On and off since yesterday; the tightness has not fully gone.
present_illness.severity: 4 out of 10 at rest, 7 out of 10 when she takes a deep breath.
present_illness.timing: Worse on deep breathing and when she walks.
present_illness.aggravating: Deep breaths, coughing, climbing the stairs to her flat.
present_illness.relieving: Nothing much. Breathing slowly into her hands did not help this time, which surprised her.
associated: heart feels like it is racing
more breathless than usual climbing stairs for about four days
coughed once yesterday and saw a small streak of blood
present_illness.progression: The breathlessness has been building for four days; the chest pain started yesterday.

past_medical: Diagnosed with generalised anxiety two years ago, has had several panic attacks
medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill daily for the last three years
family: An aunt had 'a clot in the leg' after an operation
No family history of heart attacks
social: Flew back from a 9-hour work trip five days ago, window seat, did not get up
Sits at a desk 10 hours a day
review_of_systems_positive: left calf has felt achy and tight for a few days, she assumed it was from the gym
sleeping badly because of work stress
review_of_systems_negative: no ankle swelling that she has noticed
no pregnancy, last period was normal and two weeks ago

examination.label: Vital signs
examination.result: Pulse 104/min regular. BP 118/72 mmHg. Respiratory rate 24/min. SpO2 94% on room air (96% when the nurse checked at triage while she was sitting still). Temperature 37.4 C.

examination.label: General examination
examination.result: Anxious, mildly tachypnoeic at rest, speaking in full sentences. Fine tremor of the outstretched hands. No pallor, no cyanosis, no clubbing.

examination.label: Cardiovascular examination
examination.result: Regular tachycardia. Heart sounds normal; a loud P2 is appreciable. No murmur, no rub.

examination.label: Jugular venous pressure
examination.result: Just visible at 4 cm above the sternal angle — borderline raised.

examination.label: Respiratory examination
examination.result: Equal air entry. A soft pleural rub at the right base. No crackles, no wheeze, resonant throughout.

examination.label: Lower limb examination
examination.result: Left calf 3 cm greater in circumference than the right, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. Tender along the deep calf. No erythema, no cord palpable, no pitting oedema.

examination.label: Thyroid examination
examination.result: No goitre, no bruit, no lid lag.

investigations.label: 12-lead ECG
investigations.result: Sinus tachycardia at 106/min. T-wave inversion in V1 to V3. Incomplete right bundle branch block. No S1Q3T3 pattern. No ST elevation.

investigations.label: Arterial blood gas
investigations.result: pH 7.49, PaO2 68 mmHg, PaCO2 29 mmHg, HCO3 22 on room air. Alveolar-arterial gradient widened.

investigations.label: CT pulmonary angiogram
investigations.result: Filling defects in the right lower lobe segmental and subsegmental pulmonary arteries. Right ventricle to left ventricle diameter ratio 0.95. No infarction. No alternative pathology.

investigations.label: Doppler ultrasound of the legs
investigations.result: Non-compressible left popliteal and femoral veins with echogenic thrombus. Right leg normal.

investigations.label: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Normal heart size, clear lung fields, no consolidation, no pneumothorax, no effusion.

investigations.label: High-sensitivity troponin
investigations.result: Troponin I 46 ng/L (upper reference limit 34) — mildly elevated, static on repeat.

investigations.label: Transthoracic echocardiogram
investigations.result: Mildly dilated right ventricle with preserved systolic function (TAPSE 19 mm). Estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 42 mmHg. No septal flattening. Left ventricle normal.

investigations.label: Renal function and electrolytes
investigations.result: Urea 22 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, Na 139, K 4.0 mEq/L.

differentials.why: Four risk factors (long-haul flight, combined oral contraceptive, prolonged sitting, family history), pleuritic pain with haemoptysis, hypoxia with a widened A-a gradient, an asymmetric tender calf, right-heart strain on ECG and echo, and a confirmed filling defect.
The source. Confirmed on Doppler; the two diagnoses are one disease and must be named together.

The patient's own explanation and the trap in this case. Panic does not cause hypoxia, haemoptysis, a pleural rub, an asymmetric calf or right-heart strain. It must be a diagnosis of exclusion, never an anchor.

The mildly raised troponin has to be explained. Here it reflects right ventricular strain, not coronary occlusion — the pain is pleuritic, the pattern is anterior T inversion with incomplete RBBB, and the troponin is static.
Sudden pleuritic pain with breathlessness. Excluded by equal air entry, resonance and a normal chest X-ray.
A pleural rub with a low-grade temperature could fit, but there is no productive cough, no consolidation and no leucocytosis.
Tachycardia with a fine tremor and anxiety is worth a TSH, but it does not explain the hypoxia or the calf.
No reproducible chest-wall tenderness, and it does not cause desaturation.

final_diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism (submassive / intermediate-risk, with right ventricular dilatation and a mildly raised troponin) arising from a left lower-limb deep vein thrombosis, provoked by long-haul travel and combined oral contraceptive use — presenting in a patient with a prior diagnosis of anxiety
diagnosis_reasoning: The pre-existing anxiety diagnosis is a distractor. Four independent thrombotic risk factors were present. The pain is pleuritic rather than central, there was haemoptysis, and the breathlessness preceded the pain by four days — none of which fits panic. Objective signs that anxiety cannot produce: SpO2 94% with a widened A-a gradient, a pleural rub, a 3 cm calf asymmetry, a loud P2, and anterior T-wave inversion with incomplete RBBB. The CTPA confirms segmental emboli and the echo shows right ventricular dilatation, placing her in the intermediate-risk category rather than low-risk.

history.label: Relation of the pain to breathing
history.teaching_note: Pleuritic pain moves the differential to the pleura and the pulmonary vasculature, away from panic.

history.label: Recent travel or prolonged immobility
history.teaching_note: The single highest-yield question in this case. She will not volunteer the flight.

history.label: Contraceptive and hormone use
history.teaching_note: Combined oral contraceptives raise VTE risk three- to five-fold. Always ask a woman of reproductive age about them by name.

history.label: Leg pain or swelling
history.teaching_note: Asks directly for the source of the embolus. Her calf ache was dismissed as a gym injury.

history.label: Blood in the sputum
history.teaching_note: Haemoptysis with pleuritic pain suggests pulmonary infarction.

history.label: Breathlessness and its time course
history.teaching_note: Four days of progressive exertional breathlessness preceding the pain does not fit a panic attack.

history.label: How this episode compares with her previous panic attacks
history.teaching_note: Asking a patient whether this feels like their usual episode is one of the cheapest and most powerful anti-anchoring questions in medicine.

history.label: Light-headedness or syncope
history.teaching_note: Syncope in pulmonary embolism implies haemodynamic significance.

history.label: Personal or family history of clots
history.teaching_note: A first-degree family history raises suspicion of an inherited thrombophilia.

history.label: Pregnancy and menstrual history
history.teaching_note: Changes both the risk assessment and every imaging decision that follows.

history.label: Recent surgery, trauma or malignancy
history.teaching_note: Completes the Wells score risk factors.

history.label: Fever and infective symptoms
history.teaching_note: Pulmonary embolism can produce a low-grade fever; it does not exclude the diagnosis.

examination.label: Vital signs including oxygen saturation
examination.teaching_note: SpO2 94% at rest is the finding that anxiety cannot explain. Anyone who skips it will anchor on panic.

examination.label: Both legs, with calf circumference compared
examination.teaching_note: A 3 cm difference scores in the Wells DVT criteria and points straight to the source.

examination.label: Respiratory examination
examination.teaching_note: A pleural rub is an objective sign; it also excludes pneumothorax when combined with normal percussion.

examination.label: Cardiovascular examination
examination.teaching_note: A loud P2 signals raised pulmonary artery pressure.

examination.label: Jugular venous pressure
examination.teaching_note: A raised JVP with clear lungs is the classic combination in pulmonary embolism.

investigations.label: ECG
investigations.teaching_note: Anterior T-wave inversion with incomplete RBBB is right-heart strain, not ischaemia. S1Q3T3 is neither sensitive nor common.

investigations.label: D-dimer
investigations.teaching_note: Useful only to rule out in low-probability patients. With a high Wells score, proceed to imaging whatever it shows.

investigations.label: CT pulmonary angiogram
investigations.teaching_note: The confirmatory test. Withholding it because 'she has anxiety' is the error this case is built around.

investigations.label: Chest X-ray
investigations.teaching_note: Usually normal in pulmonary embolism; its job here is to exclude pneumothorax and consolidation.

investigations.label: Arterial blood gas
investigations.teaching_note: A widened A-a gradient with hypocapnia distinguishes true hypoxia from hyperventilation.

investigations.label: Doppler ultrasound of the legs
investigations.teaching_note: Confirms the source, and in pregnancy can secure the diagnosis without radiation.

investigations.label: Troponin
investigations.teaching_note: Here it is a risk-stratification tool, not a coronary test — it separates low-risk from intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism.

investigations.label: Echocardiogram
investigations.teaching_note: Right ventricular dilatation defines submassive pulmonary embolism and changes monitoring and treatment.

investigations.label: Pregnancy test
investigations.teaching_note: Mandatory before CT in any woman of reproductive age.

investigations.label: Thyroid function
investigations.teaching_note: Reasonable to check given the tremor and tachycardia, but it must not delay imaging.

hints: She gave you an explanation before you examined her. Which of your findings does that explanation fail to account for?
Two objective findings here cannot be produced by anxiety at all. Look again at the saturation and at the legs.
Review the risk factors for clot formation in a young woman on hormonal contraception, and the clinical scoring tool used to decide who needs imaging for chest pain with breathlessness.
teaching_points: Premature closure on a patient's own explanation — especially a psychiatric one — is the commonest diagnostic error in emergency medicine. Anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion in anyone who is hypoxic.
Ask every patient with recurrent episodes whether this one felt the same as the others. A 'no' is a red flag.
Combined oral contraceptives plus long-haul travel is a classic provoked-VTE combination in a young woman.
A normal chest X-ray is expected in pulmonary embolism and never excludes it.
A raised troponin in pulmonary embolism reflects right ventricular strain, not coronary occlusion — but it does mean a worse prognosis.
Measure both calves. Eyeballing them misses a 3 cm difference.
